newsitem.title: USA: Surging stock market sends deficit plunging.
newsitem.headline: Surging stock market sends deficit plunging.

text.p: Bulging tax receipts gave the government a record surplus of $93.94 billion during April, the Treasury Department said on Wednesday, raising prospects for a dramatically lower deficit for the full year.

With April 15 marking the deadline for individuals to file their 1996 tax returns, the monthly surplus this year outstripped by 30 percent the $72.4-billion surplus posted a year earlier, in April 1996. It followed a $21.32 billion deficit in March.

Revenues, principally from taxes but also from fees and other sources, hit a record $228.59 billion in April. That was more than double the $108.1 billion taken in during March and well ahead of April 1996 revenues of $203.47 billion.
Treasury cited "the impact of large individual tax deposits" as the cause of the record revenues and surplus in April.

During the first seven months of fiscal 1997, which ends Sept. 30, the cumulative budget deficit plummeted 69 percent to $16.9 billion from $55.31 billion in the comparable first seven months of fiscal 1996.
Kathleen Stephansen, an economist with Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York, said the April figures "present a very impressive picture for the full year."

Stephansen estimated the fiscal 1997 budget deficit could fall to $76 billion, or barely 1 percent of the value of gross domestic product, down from 1.4 percent in fiscal 1996, when the total deficit was $107.45 billion.

"You would have to go back to 1973 or 1974 to see a ratio this low," she said, adding that the exceptionally strong performance owes much to soaring stock prices that put more taxable wealth in taxpayers' pockets.

That means much of the current improvement is cyclical, however, and so could be quickly weakened by a falloff in stock prices or by a less-robust pace of economic activity, as is widely expected later this year.
Total government outlays in April were $134.65 billion, up from $129.42 billion in March and also up from $131.06 billion a year earlier in April 1996.

Receipts from individual income taxes totaled $134.29 billion in April this year, up from $107.51 billion in April 1996. Corporate income tax receipts rose to $27.42 billion this April from $24.94 billion in April 1996.

Stephansen noted that the pickup in corporate tax payments during April was potentially significant. Most corporations completed their 1996 tax liability payments in March, so higher April payments reflect their initial forecasts for 1997.
"The implication is that corporations see a fairly bright outlook for their profits this year," Stephansen said.

The Clinton administration has officially forecast a budget deficit for the full 1997 fiscal year of $125.59 billion, up from $107.45 billion in fiscal 1996. But that estimate clearly is high in view of the strong performance during the first seven months of the tax year.

White House and congressional negotiators currently are working out details of a budget agreement to govern $1.5 trillion in government spending in the coming 1998 fiscal year and to set out goals for completely eliminating the deficit and bringing the budget into balance by 2002.
